outputs.L2:
Electrosurgical systems and techniques described in this disclosure employ a multi-stage power conversion arrangement to produce electrosurgical energy. These systems include an electrosurgical generator with a power converter connected to a source of electrical energy and arranged to generate the electrosurgical energy.

The power converter has a boost converter that changes a first direct current supplied by the electrical energy source into a second direct current. It also includes a phase-shifted pulse width modulation (PS-PWM) resonant inverter that converts the second direct current into alternating current.

The electrosurgical generator further includes multiple sensors that detect the voltage and current of the electrosurgical energy being produced, as well as a controller connected to both the power converter and the sensors. The controller contains a signal processor that calculates tissue impedance from the measured voltage and current. It also includes an output controller that chooses one of several output characteristics based on the calculated tissue impedance and produces control signals for regulating the boost converter and the PS-PWM resonant inverter in accordance with the chosen output characteristic.
outputs.L3:
The disclosed electrosurgical systems generate electrosurgical energy using a multi-stage power converter architecture. This architecture is configured to receive electrical energy from a source and condition that energy into a form suitable for delivery to tissue through an electrosurgical instrument.

In one implementation, an electrosurgical generator includes a power converter electrically coupled to an electrical energy source. The electrical energy source may provide an initial direct current input to the power converter. The power converter includes a boost converter stage that converts the first direct current into a second direct current having a desired voltage level. This boosted direct current provides an intermediate power supply for subsequent conversion.

The power converter further includes an inverter stage, such as a phase-shifted pulse width modulation resonant inverter. The resonant inverter receives the second direct current from the boost converter and converts it into alternating current. The alternating current is then used to generate electrosurgical energy suitable for cutting, coagulating, sealing, or otherwise treating tissue.

The electrosurgical generator also includes a controller configured to monitor operation of the system and regulate the output of the power converter. The controller receives sensed voltage and current information associated with the electrosurgical output and determines tissue impedance based on those sensed values. Using the determined tissue impedance, together with a selected output characteristic, the controller controls operation of the boost converter and the resonant inverter. In this manner, the system can adjust the generated electrosurgical energy to achieve a desired output response during treatment.
outputs.L4:
An electrosurgical generator is configured to produce controlled radio-frequency energy for use in electrosurgical procedures such as cutting, coagulation, sealing, desiccation, or ablation of tissue. The generator includes a multi-stage power conversion architecture designed to efficiently convert input power into a regulated electrosurgical output. In one implementation, the power conversion system includes a boost converter stage followed by a phase-shifted pulse width modulation resonant inverter stage. The boost converter receives power from a power source and raises or regulates the intermediate DC bus voltage to a desired level. The resonant inverter then converts the regulated DC voltage into a high-frequency AC waveform suitable for delivery to an electrosurgical instrument.

The generator further includes voltage and current sensing circuitry positioned to monitor electrical conditions associated with the output delivered to the surgical instrument and the tissue being treated. These sensors may measure output voltage, output current, phase relationship, delivered power, or other electrical parameters. The sensed signals are provided to a controller, which may include a microprocessor, digital signal processor, field-programmable gate array, analog control circuitry, or a combination of such components. The controller processes the sensed voltage and current information and uses it to regulate operation of the boost converter and the resonant inverter.

During use, the electrosurgical instrument applies energy to tissue, and the electrical response of the tissue changes depending on tissue type, hydration level, contact pressure, temperature, and the progression of the surgical effect. The controller determines tissue impedance based at least in part on the sensed voltage and current. For example, the controller may calculate impedance as a function of measured output voltage and measured output current. The determined impedance provides an indication of the load presented by the tissue and allows the generator to adjust the energy output in real time.

Based on the determined tissue impedance and other sensed operating conditions, the controller selects or modifies one or more output characteristics of the generator. These output characteristics may include output voltage, output current, output power, duty cycle, frequency, pulse duration, crest factor, waveform shape, or energy delivery mode. The controller may operate the boost converter to control the DC bus voltage and may operate the phase-shifted pulse width modulation resonant inverter to control the amplitude, timing, and delivery of the high-frequency electrosurgical waveform. By coordinating these stages, the generator can provide precise and efficient regulation over a wide range of tissue impedances and surgical conditions.

The system may dynamically adjust energy delivery as tissue impedance changes during a procedure. For instance, when tissue impedance is low, the generator may limit current to prevent excessive heating or arcing. As impedance increases due to tissue drying, coagulation, or sealing, the generator may increase voltage, reduce current, alter pulse timing, or otherwise modify the waveform to maintain a desired surgical effect. The controller may also compare sensed parameters with predetermined thresholds, control profiles, or treatment algorithms to determine when to increase, decrease, interrupt, or terminate energy delivery.

This closed-loop regulation enables the generator to deliver electrosurgical energy more accurately and consistently than systems operating with fixed output settings. By continuously monitoring voltage and current, determining tissue impedance, and selecting appropriate output characteristics, the generator can adapt to changing tissue conditions and instrument loading. As a result, the system can improve electrosurgical performance by enhancing cutting efficiency, promoting reliable coagulation or sealing, reducing thermal spread, minimizing unintended tissue damage, and improving overall procedural control.
outputs.L5:
The PWM, or Pulse Width Modulation, is a technique used to control the amount of power delivered to an electronic device. Instead of changing the voltage directly, PWM rapidly switches a signal on and off. By adjusting the amount of time the signal stays on compared to the time it stays off, the average power can be increased or decreased.

PWM is commonly used in many applications, such as controlling the speed of motors, dimming LED lights, and managing power in electronic circuits. For example, if an LED receives a PWM signal that is on 50% of the time and off 50% of the time, it will appear to shine at about half brightness. If the signal is on 90% of the time, the LED will appear much brighter.

The main advantage of PWM is efficiency. Since the device is either fully on or fully off, less energy is wasted as heat compared to methods that reduce power by using resistance. This makes PWM especially useful in battery-powered devices and systems where energy efficiency is important.

In modern electronics, PWM is a simple but powerful method for precise control. Whether in robotics, lighting systems, fans, or motor drivers, the PWM plays an important role in making devices more efficient and responsive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in formal technical language, an electrosurgical system with a multi-stage power converter and a controller that adjusts output characteristics based on measured tissue impedance.
counterfactuals.output:
An electrosurgical system includes an electrosurgical generator configured to deliver radio-frequency (RF) energy to tissue through an electrosurgical instrument, and a control architecture configured to regulate the delivered energy as a function of measured tissue impedance.

The generator includes a multi-stage power conversion circuit. A first conversion stage is configured to receive input power from an AC mains source or a DC supply and generate an intermediate DC bus voltage. The first conversion stage may include an AC-to-DC rectifier, power-factor-correction circuitry, and/or a regulated DC-DC converter. A second conversion stage is coupled to the intermediate DC bus and is configured to generate a high-frequency therapeutic output signal. The second conversion stage may include an inverter, resonant converter, switching bridge, transformer, and output filtering or matching network configured to provide an RF electrosurgical waveform to active and return electrodes or to opposing jaws of a bipolar instrument.

The system further includes voltage and current sensing circuitry operatively coupled to the output of the generator. The sensing circuitry is configured to measure, directly or indirectly, an output voltage and an output current associated with the RF energy delivered to tissue. A tissue impedance determination circuit or processor computes a tissue impedance value based on the measured voltage and current, including one or more of magnitude, phase angle, real component, reactive component, or a time-varying impedance profile.

A controller is coupled to the multi-stage power conversion circuit and to the sensing circuitry. The controller includes processing circuitry and memory storing executable control instructions. The controller is configured to monitor the measured tissue impedance during delivery of electrosurgical energy and to adjust one or more output characteristics of the generator in response to the measured impedance. The adjusted output characteristics may include output power, output voltage, output current, duty cycle, switching frequency, pulse width, crest factor, modulation pattern, RF burst duration, or an operating mode of the generator.

In operation, the controller may regulate the first conversion stage to vary the intermediate DC bus voltage and regulate the second conversion stage to shape the RF output waveform. For example, when the measured tissue impedance is below a predetermined threshold, the controller may limit output current or reduce bus voltage to prevent excessive current density. When the measured tissue impedance increases, indicating tissue desiccation, coagulation progression, or reduced conductive coupling, the controller may increase voltage compliance, reduce power, alter pulse timing, or terminate energy delivery. The controller may compare the measured impedance or a derivative thereof to one or more thresholds, profiles, or control curves to determine an appropriate adjustment.

The controller may implement closed-loop control in which the tissue impedance is repeatedly sampled during activation of the electrosurgical instrument, and converter operating parameters are updated in real time. The first conversion stage may provide coarse regulation of available energy by controlling the DC bus, while the second conversion stage may provide fine regulation of the RF waveform delivered to the load. This multi-stage regulation enables the system to maintain a selected therapeutic effect over a range of tissue conditions while reducing arcing, thermal spread, sticking, or unintended tissue damage.

The electrosurgical instrument may be monopolar or bipolar. In a monopolar configuration, RF energy is delivered from an active electrode through patient tissue to a return electrode. In a bipolar configuration, RF energy is delivered between first and second electrodes disposed on the instrument, such as electrodes on opposing jaw members. The system may further include user input controls for selecting a cutting, coagulation, sealing, or blended mode, and the controller may apply different impedance-response algorithms depending on the selected mode.

The system may also include safety circuitry configured to disable or limit output upon detection of an abnormal condition, including excessive impedance, insufficient impedance, open-circuit operation, short-circuit operation, electrode fault, return electrode fault, excessive temperature, or converter overcurrent. The controller may store measured impedance data and control parameters for diagnostic, calibration, or procedural logging purposes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a summary of the present disclosure for a medical electrosurgical energy generator including a boost stage, PS-PWM inverter stage, sensors, signal processor, and output controller.
counterfactuals.output:
The present disclosure relates to a medical electrosurgical energy generator configured to deliver controlled electrosurgical energy to a surgical instrument for cutting, coagulating, sealing, ablating, or otherwise treating tissue. In one aspect, the generator includes a power conversion architecture having a boost stage configured to receive an input supply and generate a regulated intermediate DC bus voltage. The boost stage may be controlled to adjust the DC bus voltage according to a selected treatment mode, tissue response, requested output power, or operating condition of the generator.

The generator further includes an inverter stage coupled to the boost stage. The inverter stage may be implemented as a phase-shift pulse-width modulation (PS-PWM) inverter configured to convert the DC bus voltage into a high-frequency electrosurgical output waveform. By controlling a phase shift, duty cycle, switching frequency, or a combination thereof, the PS-PWM inverter stage can regulate the magnitude, power, crest factor, or waveform characteristics of the electrosurgical energy delivered to a patient load.

One or more sensors are provided to monitor operating parameters of the generator and/or the electrosurgical output. The sensors may include voltage sensors, current sensors, temperature sensors, bus voltage sensors, output impedance sensors, leakage current sensors, or other monitoring circuitry. Sensor signals may represent generator conditions, output voltage, output current, delivered power, tissue impedance, tissue state changes, or fault conditions.

A signal processor is coupled to the sensors and configured to receive and process the sensed signals. The signal processor may determine electrosurgical output parameters, calculate tissue impedance or power delivery, detect arcing or open-circuit conditions, identify short-circuit or over-temperature conditions, and generate control information based on the sensed operating state. The signal processor may also compare measured values with target values associated with a selected electrosurgical mode or treatment profile.

An output controller is operatively coupled to the signal processor, boost stage, and PS-PWM inverter stage. The output controller is configured to regulate electrosurgical energy delivery by controlling the boost stage and/or inverter stage in response to processed sensor information. The output controller may adjust the DC bus voltage generated by the boost stage and control the PS-PWM inverter stage to maintain a desired output voltage, current, power, impedance response, waveform shape, or treatment endpoint. In certain implementations, the output controller coordinates coarse regulation through the boost stage and fine or dynamic regulation through the PS-PWM inverter stage.

The disclosed generator may provide improved control of electrosurgical output energy, enhanced response to changing tissue impedance, reduced switching losses, improved efficiency, and increased safety through continuous monitoring and closed-loop control. The system may further include fault detection and protective shutdown features configured to disable or limit output energy upon detection of unsafe operating conditions. Accordingly, the present disclosure provides an electrosurgical generator capable of delivering accurately regulated, mode-specific electrosurgical energy using coordinated boost conversion, PS-PWM inversion, sensing, signal processing, and output control.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a patent specification paragraph explaining systems and methods for producing electrosurgical energy using sensed voltage/current feedback and tissue impedance calculations.
counterfactuals.output: In some embodiments, an electrosurgical generator is configured to produce electrosurgical energy for delivery to tissue through an electrosurgical instrument, the generator including an energy source, an output stage, and a controller operatively coupled to one or more voltage and current sensing circuits. During activation, the sensing circuits sample a voltage waveform and a current waveform associated with the delivered electrosurgical energy, and the controller determines a tissue impedance based at least in part on the sensed voltage and current, for example by calculating an instantaneous, average, RMS, complex, or phase-adjusted impedance value. The controller may compare the determined tissue impedance, and/or changes in the determined tissue impedance over time, to one or more thresholds, profiles, or control parameters corresponding to a selected operating mode, such as cutting, coagulation, sealing, or vessel fusion. Based on the comparison, the controller adjusts one or more output characteristics of the electrosurgical energy, including voltage, current, power, duty cycle, pulse width, crest factor, frequency, waveform shape, or activation duration, to regulate energy delivery to the tissue. In certain embodiments, the controller repeatedly or continuously updates the impedance calculation from the sensed feedback signals and modifies the output in real time to maintain a target power level, limit peak voltage or current, detect tissue state transitions, compensate for changing tissue conditions, reduce arcing, or terminate energy delivery when a completion condition is detected. The systems and methods thereby provide closed-loop control of electrosurgical energy using sensed voltage/current feedback and tissue impedance calculations to improve consistency, efficiency, and safety of tissue treatment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a concise invention overview for an electrosurgical generator architecture where a controller manages both a DC-DC boost converter and a resonant inverter according to selected output characteristics.
counterfactuals.output:
An electrosurgical generator architecture includes a controller operatively coupled to both a DC-DC boost converter and a resonant inverter. The boost converter receives an input supply and produces a controllable DC bus voltage, while the resonant inverter converts the DC bus into a high-frequency electrosurgical output delivered to a surgical instrument or patient load.

The controller selects or receives desired output characteristics, such as operating mode, target power, voltage, current, waveform shape, crest factor, or tissue-effect profile. Based on those selected characteristics and feedback representative of the generator output or load condition, the controller coordinates operation of the boost converter and the resonant inverter. For example, the controller may adjust the DC bus voltage through the boost converter while independently controlling inverter switching frequency, phase, duty cycle, burst timing, or resonance operation to regulate the delivered electrosurgical energy.

This coordinated control allows the generator to efficiently produce multiple electrosurgical output modes, maintain stable energy delivery over changing tissue impedance, improve dynamic response, and reduce stress on power-stage components by distributing regulation between the upstream DC-DC stage and the downstream resonant inverter.
